meta_title: Set Your Server's IP Address in Access Keys | VpnHood!
meta_description: Choose the IP address VpnHood! SERVER listens on and the one it puts in access keys, on a managed server in VpnHood! MANAGER or on a standalone one.
title: Set your server's IP addresses
lead: An access key tells apps which address to connect to. The server usually works that out by itself, but on a machine with more than one IP address you may need to set it: the address the server listens on, and the address it puts in the keys.
auto_title: How the server finds its address
auto_listen: By default, the server listens on every address of the machine, on TCP port [server_port].
auto_keys: For the keys, it looks its address up through its own outgoing traffic: it asks a web service which address that traffic comes from.
auto_when: That finds the right address on most machines. Set it yourself when:
when_outgoing: The machine sends its traffic from another address than the one users should connect to, such as a separate outgoing IP. The lookup would find the outgoing one.
when_several: The machine has more than one public IP address, and the keys should carry a particular one.
when_lookup: The lookup fails, for example because the machine cannot reach the web service. A standalone server then does not start, and its log says [log_public_endpoints]
mgr_box_title: Easily manage your servers' addresses with VpnHood! MANAGER
mgr_box_desc: Instead of editing the file below, let the free web panel find each server's address by itself, and change it with a few clicks when you need another.
file_desc: The server reads its settings from [server_appsettings]. A new install has no such file: create it, and from then on the server uses it in place of the settings it was installed with. Two settings under [setting_file_access_manager] decide the addresses:
file_tcp: [setting_tcp_endpoints] lists the addresses and ports the server listens on.
file_public: [setting_public_endpoints] lists the addresses and ports that go into access keys. Use real addresses only: [ip_any_v4] or [ip_any_v6] here stops the server from starting.
caption_file: The whole file: the server listens on every address and puts [ip_connection_example] in the keys
file_one_ip: To listen on one address only, as with a separate outgoing IP, put that address in [setting_tcp_endpoints] as well. Outside Docker, the server adds an address it listens on to the machine's network by itself, if the machine does not have it yet.
file_nat: On a cloud where the machine has only private addresses, such as AWS, Google Cloud, Azure or Oracle Cloud, listen on the private address, or on every address, and put the public IP in [setting_public_endpoints].
file_restart: Then restart the server with [server_restart_linux], or with [docker_restart] in Docker. To check, create a key with [vhserver_gen]: the line [hostendpoints_label] shows the addresses it carries.
file_udp: UDP listens on the addresses of TCP by default. If you set [setting_udp_endpoints] or [setting_quic_endpoints] yourself, give them the same address as TCP.
file_udp_port: Devices set to UDP need the server's UDP port open too, in the machine's firewall and your hosting provider's. The server picks the port at its first start, and its log names it.
keys_title: Keys you have already given out
keys_desc: A key carries the addresses it was made with, so an app holding an older key keeps trying the old address. Each app picks up the current key by itself whenever it connects, so after a change, keep the server listening on the old address for a few days, then remove it.
keys_how: Keep the old address in [setting_tcp_endpoints] only, so the server still listens on it but no longer puts it in the keys.
keys_lost: An app that can no longer reach the old address needs a new key from you. Behind a reverse proxy, apps connect to the proxy, so your server's address can change without breaking their keys.
